title: How Birds Find Their Way
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every autumn, billions of birds leave the regions where they have bred and travel to warmer parts of the world, returning the following spring. Some of these journeys are astonishing. The Arctic tern flies from the far north to the Antarctic and back each year, and a bar-tailed godwit fitted with a satellite tag has been tracked flying from Alaska to New Zealand, a distance of more than eleven thousand kilometres, without once stopping to rest or feed. How birds find their way across oceans and deserts, often at night and often to the very same nesting site they used the year before, has been investigated for more than seventy years. The answer has turned out to be not one sense but several.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first breakthrough came in Germany in the early 1950s. Gustav Kramer noticed that caged starlings became restless at migration time and hopped repeatedly towards the direction in which they would normally fly – but only when they could see the sun. When he used mirrors to change the apparent position of the sun, the birds shifted their direction to match. Since the sun moves across the sky during the day, a bird using it as a guide must also keep track of the time, and later experiments confirmed that birds whose internal clocks had been artificially reset made exactly the errors that would be expected.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Most small birds, however, migrate at night. In the 1960s the American biologist Stephen Emlen placed indigo buntings in a planetarium, where the pattern of stars on the ceiling could be altered at will. He found that the birds oriented themselves by the stars, but not, as had been supposed, by recognising particular constellations. Young buntings learn instead to identify the one point in the night sky around which all the other stars appear to rotate, which lies above the North Pole. Birds raised under an artificial sky that had been made to rotate around a different star treated that star as their guide.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Neither the sun nor the stars can explain how birds keep their course under thick cloud. In Frankfurt, Wolfgang Wiltschko surrounded caged European robins with electric coils that allowed him to alter the magnetic field around them. When he turned the field, the robins turned too. It was the first clear evidence that an animal could detect the earth's magnetism. Further work showed that the robins' compass does not distinguish north from south as a human compass does. It responds instead to the angle at which the lines of the magnetic field meet the ground, which is steep near the poles and flat at the equator.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: A compass, though, is only half of what a traveller needs. Knowing which way is south is of little use to a bird that does not know where it is. In a famous experiment in the 1950s, the Dutch researcher Ab Perdeck caught thousands of starlings as they passed through the Netherlands on their way to Britain and northern France, and transported them by aeroplane to Switzerland, several hundred kilometres to the south-east, where they were released. The adult birds, which had made the journey before, corrected for the displacement and reached their usual wintering grounds. The young birds, on their first migration, simply continued in their original direction and ended up in Spain. Young birds, it seems, inherit a direction; experienced ones possess something closer to a map.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: What that map consists of is still debated. One candidate is smell. The Italian zoologist Floriano Papi found that homing pigeons whose sense of smell had been blocked were far less successful at returning to their lofts from unfamiliar places, and proposed that birds learn the characteristic odours carried on winds from different directions. Similar results have since been obtained with seabirds, which cross vast stretches of apparently featureless ocean. Other researchers believe that small variations in the strength of the earth's magnetic field from place to place could provide information about position.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Much remains uncertain – above all, how the magnetic sense actually works. One theory holds that it depends on light-sensitive molecules in the bird's eye, so that a robin may in some sense see the magnetic field; another points to tiny particles of iron-containing minerals in the beak. The evidence for each is incomplete. What is clear is that birds do not rely on any single system. They appear to check one source of information against another, using the setting sun, for example, to adjust their magnetic compass before departing at dusk. It is this ability to combine several imperfect instruments that makes their navigation so reliable.

groups.instruction:
Look at the following findings (Questions 14–18) and the list of researchers below.
Match each finding with the correct researcher, A–E.
groups.limit: Write the correct letter, A–E, next to Questions 14–18.

items.text: Whether birds can correct their route after being moved off course depends on their experience.
Birds brought up in altered conditions will adopt a guide different from the natural one.
Birds deprived of one of their senses had difficulty finding their way home.
There was firm proof, for the first time, that an animal can sense magnetism.
The direction birds chose could be changed by altering where a source of light appeared to be.

groups.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 2?
groups.limit:
Write
TRUE if the statement agrees with the information
FALSE if the statement contradicts the information
NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this

items.text: The godwit tracked from Alaska to New Zealand made several stops on the way.
Birds that use the sun to find direction also need a sense of time.
Indigo buntings find their direction by recognising particular constellations.
Homing pigeons have a better sense of smell than seabirds do.

groups.limit: Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.

rows.text: The magnetic compass of the robin detects the {23} at which the earth's magnetic field lines meet the ground.
The young starlings that were released in Switzerland finished their journey in {24}.
Papi suggested that birds learn the {25} which winds bring from different directions.
According to one theory, the magnetic sense depends on particles in the beak of minerals containing {26}.

questions.explain:
答案是 D（Ab Perdeck）。他把椋鳥從荷蘭空運到瑞士：飛過這條路線的成鳥 corrected for the displacement，第一次遷徙的幼鳥卻照原方向飛，最後到了西班牙。
同義轉換：displacement ＝ being moved off course；had made the journey before ＝ experience。
questions.quote: The adult birds, which had made the journey before, corrected for the displacement and reached their usual wintering grounds.

questions.explain:
答案是 B（Stephen Emlen）。在繞著另一顆星旋轉的人造星空下養大的鳥，treated that star as their guide。
同義轉換：raised under an artificial sky ＝ brought up in altered conditions；a different star ＝ a guide different from the natural one。
questions.quote: Birds raised under an artificial sky that had been made to rotate around a different star treated that star as their guide.

questions.explain:
答案是 E（Floriano Papi）。嗅覺被阻斷的信鴿，從陌生地點飛回鴿舍的成功率低很多。
同義轉換：sense of smell had been blocked ＝ deprived of one of their senses；returning to their lofts ＝ finding their way home。
questions.quote: homing pigeons whose sense of smell had been blocked were far less successful at returning to their lofts from unfamiliar places

questions.explain:
答案是 C（Wolfgang Wiltschko）。他用電線圈改變知更鳥周圍的磁場，鳥跟著轉向，這是 the first clear evidence that an animal could detect the earth's magnetism。
同義轉換：first clear evidence ＝ firm proof for the first time；detect ＝ sense。
questions.quote: It was the first clear evidence that an animal could detect the earth's magnetism.

questions.explain:
答案是 A（Gustav Kramer）。他用鏡子改變太陽看起來的位置，鳥就跟著改變方向。
陷阱：Emlen 也改變了天空，但他改的是星星旋轉的中心，而且是養育條件。題目說的是 where a source of light appeared to be，對應 the apparent position of the sun。
questions.quote: When he used mirrors to change the apparent position of the sun, the birds shifted their direction to match.

questions.explain:
答案是 FALSE。這隻斑尾鷸飛了一萬一千多公里，without once stopping to rest or feed（一次也沒有停下來）。
解題關鍵：without once stopping 與 made several stops 直接矛盾。
questions.quote: without once stopping to rest or feed

questions.explain:
答案是 TRUE。太陽在一天之中會移動，所以用太陽當指引的鳥 must also keep track of the time。
同義轉換：keep track of the time ＝ need a sense of time。
questions.quote: a bird using it as a guide must also keep track of the time

questions.explain:
答案是 FALSE。Emlen 發現鳥確實靠星星定向，but not, as had been supposed, by recognising particular constellations，牠們學的是星空旋轉的中心點。
陷阱：題目說的正是「原本大家以為」的方式，也就是被實驗推翻的那個想法。
questions.quote: but not, as had been supposed, by recognising particular constellations

questions.explain:
答案是 NOT GIVEN。文章說信鴿的實驗和海鳥得到類似的結果（Similar results），但沒有比較兩者嗅覺的好壞。
陷阱：兩種鳥都出現在同一段，不代表文章做了比較。
questions.quote: Similar results have since been obtained with seabirds

questions.explain:
答案是 angle（角度）。知更鳥的羅盤不分南北，而是 responds instead to the angle at which the lines of the magnetic field meet the ground。
解題關鍵：空格後的 at which... meet the ground 與原文完全相同。
questions.quote: It responds instead to the angle at which the lines of the magnetic field meet the ground

questions.explain:
答案是 Spain。幼鳥照原本的方向繼續飛，ended up in Spain。
陷阱：Britain and northern France 是牠們原本的目的地，Switzerland 是被釋放的地點，都不是最後抵達的地方。
questions.quote: simply continued in their original direction and ended up in Spain

questions.explain:
答案是 odours（氣味）。Papi 提出鳥會學習 the characteristic odours carried on winds from different directions。
注意：不能填 smell，原文這裡用的字是 odours，題目要求用文章裡的字，而且空格要填複數名詞。美式拼法 odors 也算對。
questions.quote: proposed that birds learn the characteristic odours carried on winds from different directions

questions.explain:
答案是 iron（鐵）。另一個理論指向鳥喙裡 tiny particles of iron-containing minerals。
同義轉換：iron-containing minerals ＝ minerals containing iron。
陷阱：light-sensitive molecules 是另一個理論，位置在眼睛，不是鳥喙。
questions.quote: another points to tiny particles of iron-containing minerals in the beak
